transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I’m here because it’s gotten to the point where I can’t just keep ignoring it. For months now, the property manager and some people in the building have been doing these things—misdelivered mail, noises in the walls at certain times, neighbors making little comments that sound casual but aren’t.

And I know how that sounds, but I worked as a management analyst, so patterns are not exactly foreign to me. People always want to say it’s paperwork or a mix-up or “old pipes,” but when the same kinds of things keep lining up, it’s not random. It feels like they’re trying to pressure me out of my apartment, and no explanation they give really changes what I’m seeing.
Over these past several months, have you also noticed a significant change in your mood—like feeling unusually down, hopeless, or on the other end, unusually elevated, energetic, or irritable?

I don’t know that I’d call it a mood change, exactly. I mean, anybody would be bothered if this was happening where they live. It wears on you. But it’s not like I woke up one day feeling… euphoric or whatever.

Down, no—well, frustrated, yes. Irritable, maybe when the office gives me that look like I’m supposed to just accept their explanation. But that’s not a mood problem, that’s a response to what’s going on. I’ve always been pretty even-keeled. At work, people used to say I was the one who could sit with spreadsheets for hours and not get rattled—though one supervisor, years ago, he’d try to bury things in the numbers, and I caught it.

So… I don’t think I’ve noticed what you’re describing. Not in the way you mean.

Aside from the noises in the walls that others might also hear, have you ever heard voices or sounds—like someone talking about you or commenting on what you're doing—when no one else was actually there?

Voices? No, I don’t think so—not like… someone standing there talking when nobody is there.

The sounds I mean are more like the building itself, or people moving around where they shouldn’t be, and sometimes you can tell there’s a pattern to it. My old office had walls like that too—thin enough that you’d hear conversations three rooms over, and then they’d act surprised you knew what was being discussed. But that’s different from hearing a voice in an empty room.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had that. It’s the timing of the noises, and the way it lines up with everything else, that’s the issue.
Can you tell me exactly how many months ago you first started noticing these things happening, and has it been continuous since then?

It started… I’d say about 11 months ago. Pretty soon after I moved into the new apartment.

At first I thought, all right, new building, you have to learn the rhythms—every place has its sounds. The place I lived before had a radiator that would knock like someone tapping a wrench, and the landlord always had some story about steam pressure. But this was different, and it kept lining up.

So yes, it’s been going on more or less continuously since then. Not every minute of every day, obviously, but from shortly after I moved in until now.
Aside from your concerns about the building, how have things been going with your daily routine—work, relationships, and taking care of yourself—over these past 11 months?

Well, the apartment situation takes up more of my attention than I’d like, that’s true. But outside of that, I’m not falling apart or anything.

I still pay my bills, keep track of my accounts—actually I’ve always been careful with finances, from my analyst days, you know, spreadsheets, categories, reconciling things properly. I cook for myself. Nothing fancy every night, but I eat. I keep appointments if they’re on the calendar.

Work-wise, I can still talk through consulting ideas in a pretty organized way. Same with painting—if I’m focused on that, I can discuss a piece, composition, color, all of it. It’s just when the building issues intrude that everything gets dragged back there, because how could it not? But no, I’m still managing the basic parts of my life.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that the property manager and neighbors are orchestrating events to force him out of his apartment) persisting for approximately 11 months. He explicitly denies auditory or other hallucinations, denies any manic, hypomanic, or depressive mood episode, and maintains intact functioning in daily self-care, finances, cooking, and occupational/creative activities aside from preoccupation with the delusional theme. The delusion is systematized and plausible in structure (interpersonal harassment) rather than bizarre, and there is no evidence of disorganized speech/behavior, negative symptoms, or mood syndrome overlapping the psychosis. This clinical picture—circumscribed, non-bizarre delusion(s) for >1 month without other psychotic or mood symptoms and with preserved functioning outside the delusional system—meets criteria for Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia (F20.9, which requires additional psychotic symptoms and greater functional decline) or unspecified psychosis (F28).
